item.title: Nestlé to sell ice cream unit to Froneri in major overhaul
item.description:
Nestlé, the world's largest food and beverage company, announced Thursday that it will sell its remaining ice cream business to joint venture partner Froneri as part of a sweeping corporate overhaul aimed at streamlining operations around four core categories.

The Swiss giant, known for KitKat chocolate bars and Nescafé coffee, said it is in "advanced negotiations" to transfer the ice cream division, which includes brands like Häagen-Dazs, to Froneri—a joint venture Nestlé created in 2016 with private equity firm PAI Partners. Under the restructuring, the company will concentrate resources on coffee, petcare, nutrition, and food and snacks.

item.title: European stocks dip as oil surges on U.S.-Iran tensions
item.description:
European markets pulled back slightly Thursday after hitting record highs a day earlier, as investors weighed surging oil prices against escalating tensions between the United States and Iran over Tehran's nuclear program.

The pan-European Stoxx Europe 600 Index dipped 0.1% in early trading, settling around 628 points after reaching an all-time high on Wednesday. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 fell 0.3%, while Germany's DAX and France's CAC 40 each declined around 0.2% to 0.3%.

item.title: Study finds oxygen-using ancestors, solving complex life mystery
item.description:
Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have resolved a fundamental puzzle about how animals, plants, and fungi evolved, publishing findings in the journal Nature that show our ancient microbial ancestors could use oxygen, contrary to what scientists had long believed.

The discovery addresses a paradox that has troubled evolutionary biologists for years. The prevailing theory holds that all complex life, called eukaryotes, arose when two very different microbes merged billions of years ago. One of these ancestral microbes, the alphaproteobacterium that became the mitochondria, required oxygen to survive. The other, an Asgard archaeon, was thought to live exclusively in oxygen-free environments. How these two organisms came into close contact remained unexplained.

item.title: Former Prince Andrew arrested over Epstein files allegations
item.description:
Thames Valley Police arrested Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly Prince Andrew, on Thursday morning on suspicion of misconduct in public office, marking the first time in contemporary history that a senior royal has been taken into custody.

Officers in plain clothes arrived at Wood Farm on the royal Sandringham Estate in Norfolk around 8 a.m. local time and detained the 66-year-old on his birthday, according to BBC and ITV reports. Police confirmed they are conducting searches at properties in Berkshire and Norfolk as part of the investigation.

"As part of investigation, we have today arrested a man in his sixties from Norfolk on suspicion of misconduct in public office," Thames Valley Police said in a statement. In accordance with national guidelines, police declined to name the arrested individual, though multiple British outlets confirmed it was the king's younger brother.

item.title: Repsol aims to boost Venezuela oil output 50% after U.S. lifts sanctions
item.description:
Spanish energy giant Repsol disclosed Thursday that Venezuela owes it €4.55 billion ($5.37 billion), while simultaneously announcing ambitious plans to boost oil production in the South American nation by more than 50 percent within the next year following the United States' reauthorization of operations there.

The debt revelation came in Repsol's annual 2025 financial report, which shows the company is owed for commercial debt tied to oil and gas supplies, late payment interest, and €947 million in financing for its Petroquiriquire joint venture with Venezuela's state-owned PDVSA. Repsol has provisioned around €3.59 billion for these receivables over the years.

item.title: UK study finds space-based solar could compete by 2040
item.description:
Space-based solar power could become cost-competitive with traditional energy sources by 2040, according to a new UK government-commissioned feasibility study released this month. The report arrives as international momentum builds toward orbital solar demonstrations this year, potentially transforming a concept once relegated to science fiction into a practical energy solution for an increasingly power-hungry world.

The study, conducted by Frazer-Nash Consultancy, projects that the levelized cost of electricity from small-scale orbital solar plants could drop from between GBP 0.0335 and GBP 0.0595 per kilowatt-hour in 2030 to between GBP 0.0087 and GBP 0.0129 per kilowatt-hour by 2040. At those prices, space solar would be competitive with nuclear and tidal power technologies. The study found that launch costs, projected to fall to approximately GBP 550 per kilogram by 2040 in an optimistic scenario, are the most significant cost driver, accounting for more than 50% of variance in electricity costs.

item.title: Trump convenes Board of Peace as Gaza disarmament stalls
item.description:
US President Donald Trump presided over the first meeting of his Board of Peace on Thursday, convening representatives from more than 45 nations in Washington to discuss the reconstruction of Gaza and the deployment of an international peacekeeping force. The meeting, held at the renamed Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace, comes as the Israel-Hamas ceasefire remains fragile and the central challenge of disarming Hamas unresolved.

Trump announced this week that participating nations have pledged $5 billion for humanitarian relief and reconstruction efforts in Gaza, alongside commitments to deploy thousands of personnel to an International Stabilization Force aimed at maintaining security as Israeli forces withdraw from the territory.

item.title: South Korea's ex-president Yoon sentenced to life for insurrection
item.description:
Former South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol was sentenced to life in prison on Thursday after a court found him guilty of leading an insurrection through his ill-fated declaration of martial law in December 2024, ending one of the most dramatic political crises in the country's democratic history.

Presiding Judge Ji Gwi-yeon of the Seoul Central District Court ruled that Yoon "directly and proactively planned" the insurrection and acted "with the purpose of subverting the Constitution by sending the military to the National Assembly to paralyze or limit its function for a substantial amount of time." Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that Yoon bore primary responsibility for destabilizing the constitutional order and had shown no remorse.

item.title: Climate change adding 47 extra days of harmful heat in coffee regions
item.description:
The world's leading coffee-producing regions are facing an average of 47 additional days of harmful heat annually due to climate change, threatening global harvests and contributing to elevated consumer prices, according to a new analysis released Wednesday by Climate Central.

The study examined daily temperatures from 2021 to 2025 across 25 countries that represent 97% of global coffee production. Every country analyzed experienced more coffee-harming heat than would have occurred without fossil fuel pollution.

item.title: US deploys largest Middle East air force since 2003 Iraq invasion
item.description:
The United States is assembling the largest concentration of military air power in the Middle East since the 2003 invasion of Iraq, positioning dozens of advanced fighter jets and a second aircraft carrier to the region as President Donald Trump weighs potential strikes on Iran.

According to a report from The Wall Street Journal, the U.S. Air Force has moved F-35s, F-22 Raptors, F-15Es, and F-16s to Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia in recent days, based on flight-tracking data. Command-and-control aircraft essential for large air campaigns, including E-3 Airborne Warning and Control System and E-11 Battlefield Airborne Communications Node aircraft, are also inbound.

item.title: Scientists first directly measure upper-atmosphere pollution from SpaceX rocket reentry
item.description:
For the first time, researchers have directly measured pollution in Earth's upper atmosphere from a specific piece of space debris, tracing a plume of lithium vapor back to the uncontrolled reentry of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket over Europe last year.

The findings, published Thursday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, mark a milestone in understanding how the burgeoning commercial space industry may be altering atmospheric chemistry in ways scientists are only beginning to comprehend.

item.title: US commits $10 billion to Trump’s Board of Peace
item.description:
President Donald Trump convened the inaugural meeting of his Board of Peace on Thursday, announcing approximately $17 billion in total pledges for humanitarian and reconstruction efforts in war-torn Gaza. The announcement came at the U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, where representatives from more than two dozen countries gathered to formalize commitments to the controversial initiative.

Trump said the United States will contribute $10 billion to the Board of Peace, the international body he chairs under a mandate approved by the United Nations Security Council in November 2025. Nine countries — Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan, and Kuwait — collectively pledged more than $7 billion, according to AFP and Associated Press reports. Trump also announced that the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs is raising an additional $2 billion, and that Japan has committed to hosting a fundraiser.

item.title: Five nations commit troops to Gaza security force, commander says
item.description:
Five nations formally committed military personnel to the International Stabilization Force for Gaza during the inaugural Board of Peace meeting on Thursday, marking a step forward for President Donald Trump's post-war reconstruction plan for the territory.

Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, and Albania pledged troops to the ISF, while Egypt and Jordan committed to training Palestinian police, according to ISF commander Major General Jasper Jeffers, who made the announcement at the meeting in Washington.

The force will begin deploying in southern Gaza's Rafah and "expand sector by sector," Jeffers said. The long-term plan envisions 20,000 ISF troops supporting the transition of security responsibilities in the enclave as Israeli forces withdraw.

item.title: UN probe says RSF siege of El-Fasher bears 'hallmarks of genocide'
item.description:
The United Nations' independent fact-finding mission on Sudan concluded Thursday that the Rapid Support Forces' siege and capture of El-Fasher last October bears "the hallmarks of genocide" against non-Arab communities, particularly the Zaghawa and Fur ethnic groups.

The report documents a coordinated campaign of destruction following an 18-month siege that deliberately starved the city's population. RSF fighters killed more than 6,000 people between October 25 and 27, 2025, according to the UN Human Rights Office, in what investigators described as "three days of absolute horror".

item.title: Ukraine drone barrage ignites Russian oil depot after Geneva talks collapse
item.description:
Russian air defense forces intercepted 113 Ukrainian drones overnight on February 18-19, the Russian Defense Ministry reported Thursday, in one of the largest drone assaults targeting Russian territory in recent weeks. The strikes came hours after U.S.-brokered peace talks in Geneva concluded without a breakthrough.

The heaviest concentration of drone activity targeted Russia's western border regions. According to the Defense Ministry, at least 50 drones were shot down over Bryansk Oblast, 35 over Smolensk Oblast, 12 over Tver Oblast, 10 over Novgorod Oblast, four over Leningrad Oblast, and two over Kaluga Oblast.

item.title: Trump gives Iran 10 days to reach nuclear deal or face action
item.description:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the United States will determine within approximately 10 days whether to pursue military action against Iran or continue with diplomatic negotiations over Tehran's nuclear program, issuing his most direct ultimatum yet in a crisis that has seen the largest American military buildup in the Middle East since 2003.

"Good talks are being had. It's proven to be, over the years, not easy to make a meaningful deal with Iran. We have to make a meaningful deal, otherwise bad things happen," Trump said during the first meeting of his Board of Peace in Washington. "So now we may have to take a step further or may not. Maybe we're going to make a deal. You're going to be finding out over the next, probably, 10 days."

item.title: US gives IEA one year to drop net zero agenda or face withdrawal
item.description:
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued a stark ultimatum to the International Energy Agency at its ministerial meeting in Paris this week, demanding the organization abandon its net-zero emissions agenda within a year or face American withdrawal.

Speaking at the conclusion of the two-day ministerial gathering on Thursday, Wright told reporters that the US would "exert all the pressure we have" to push the IEA away from its climate-focused agenda, calling net zero a "destructive illusion" with a "zero percent chance" of being realized.

item.title: World Bank opens Gaza reconstruction fund as nations pledge $17B
item.description:
World Bank President Ajay Banga announced Thursday that the Gaza Reconstruction and Development Fund is now ready to accept donations, marking a step toward rebuilding the war-devastated Palestinian territory as nations pledge billions at the first meeting of President Donald Trump's Board of Peace in Washington.

Banga, speaking at the inaugural gathering at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace, said the fund would secure donor money while the Board of Peace directs disbursements for reconstruction and development projects in the Gaza Strip. He assured donors that "robust financial, legal and oversight mechanisms" are in place to guarantee transparency about how the money is utilized.

"The World Bank's role is that of a limited trustee," Banga explained, according to Middle East Eye. "Because of our AAA rating, we have the ability to leverage private bond money to help to create the resources we need... we can de-risk private investing."

item.title: Former Prince Andrew released after arrest in Epstein-related probe
item.description:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former Prince Andrew, was released by British police late Thursday after being held for approximately 11 hours following his arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office, Thames Valley Police confirmed.

The arrest, which occurred on Mountbatten-Windsor's 66th birthday at Wood Farm on King Charles III's Sandringham estate in Norfolk, marks the first time the former royal has been detained by police. He departed a police station in a black Range Rover Thursday evening after being released "under investigation," meaning he has neither been charged nor exonerated.

item.title: North Korea opens 9th Party Congress with Kim claiming economic success
item.description:
North Korea convened its Ninth Party Congress on Thursday, the country's largest political gathering held every five years, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).

In his opening speech, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un declared that the economy had overcome recession and the country accomplished major economic goals over the past five years, KCNA reported. The claim marks a striking contrast to the 8th Party Congress in January 2021, when Kim acknowledged that his previous five-year economic plan had failed "in almost all sectors."
